newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Triumvirate runs Russia as Yeltsin awaits surgery.
newsitem.headline: Triumvirate runs Russia as Yeltsin awaits surgery.

text.p: Russia is being ruled by a triumvirate of top officials who have stepped in to fill the vacuum left by Boris Yeltsin, but the president still wields supreme power even from his sick bed.

As Yeltsin prepares for heart surgery later this month, the three main substitutes running the Kremlin are Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, presidential administration chief Anatoly Chubais and national security head Alexander Lebed.

Russian media commentators and political analysts say none of these men can fill the president's shoes on his own, but together they should prevent the world's biggest country from drifting into chaos and anarchy.
Apparent rivalries among this troika, especially between Lebed and the other two men, should also keep any personal ambitions in check.

"I don't think there is any monopoly on power. Some questions are being handled by Chubais, some by Chernomyrdin and some by Lebed," said Viktor Kremenyuk, deputy head of the USA and Canada Institute in Moscow.

But Yeltsin's illness has raised questions about the legitimacy of any stand-in leaders. The constitution gives paramount power to the president and makes no provision for temporary substitutes other than the prime minister.
Under the constitution, if the president is incapable of carrying out his duties, the premier stands in for him.
If the head of state is unfit to work for a prolonged period for health reasons, a new election must be held within three months from the moment he stops carrying out his functions.
Kremenyuk said the absence of a real substitute for Yeltsin was dangerous. "This creates a situation of instability and unpredictability, but there is no getting away from this."
He said that out of the three substitutes, only Chernomyrdin had legal powers defined by the constitution.
"Neither Chubais nor Lebed have such powers under the constitution, but nevertheless they are responsible for important structures without which the country cannot be run."

Yeltsin, apparently still taking decisions from his country residence, is expected to undergo heart bypass surgery at an elite Moscow cardiological centre -- a common operation that should be over in a matter of hours barring complications.
Yeltsin, 65, said on Thursday that his doctors had promised him a full recovery after his planned operation, which may be followed by about a month of convalescence.
The liberal newspaper Sevodnya said Yeltsin would probably not return to the Kremlin any time soon, but there was no indication of the country drifting rudderless.
"Alexander Lebed and Anatoly Chubais, with their confident actions and statements, have demonstrated that they do not intend to allow any power vacuum," the newspaper said.
Lebed, secretary of the Kremlin's policy-making Security Council, has come up with a new initiative that has brought peace to breakaway Chechnya after almost 21 months of war.

Chubais, for his part, promised and delivered a new policy of openness concerning the president's health. He also demonstrated his influence by voicing concern over the possible impact of a new decree on taxation.
The decree, which would have taxed interest income on bank accounts and may have led to a run on banks, was repealed on Friday.
Sevodnya said Yeltsin appeared to believe that Chernomyrdin, Chubais and Lebed were capable of holding the fort temporarily. "Power cannot take a holiday or lie in hospital," Sevodnya said.
The business newspaper Kommersant-Daily said Yeltsin showed great courage in coming clean about his condition and linked the announcement to the return of Chubais from holiday.
"However, you have to remember the president's character is such that he always takes the most important decisions himself," it said.

Kremenyuk agreed that Yeltsin was still capable of formulating policy on vital issues. If he failed to recover, Lebed, who makes no secret of his presidential ambitions, was in a strong position for the succession, the analyst said.

"Lebed is a public politician and he has every chance (of being elected)," Kremenyuk said, adding that Chernomyrdin was not in the same league and might not stand against him and Chubais was more skilled as an inside operator.
